tagline.text: A foundation museum in San Miguel, Tarlac, telling the Aquino family's modern history

location.label: Location
location.text: San Miguel, Tarlac City, along Luisita Industrial Park Road (inside Hacienda Luisita)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (indoor visit, open year-round)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱400~1,200 (half day starting from Tarlac City; admission, local transport and meals)

children.text: This museum in Hacienda Luisita, San Miguel, Tarlac City honors Ninoy Aquino, Corazon Aquino and Benigno Aquino III. After a renovation that began in 2023, it reopened in February 2025 with a new exhibit wing.

The Aquino Center and Museum lets you follow the Philippines' modern history through one family's story. Its exhibits cover Senator Ninoy Aquino, who stood against the Marcos regime; Corazon Aquino, who became president through the 1986 EDSA People Power Revolution; and her son, President Benigno Aquino III (nicknamed Noynoy, or PNoy). The museum is a private institution owned and run by the Ninoy & Cory Aquino Foundation (NCAF), not a government museum.

A little background makes the exhibits much easier to read for first-time foreign visitors. Ninoy Aquino was shot at Manila International Airport on August 21, 1983, as he returned from exile, and the killing fueled opposition to the Marcos regime. His widow Corazon Aquino became president after EDSA People Power in February 1986 and served until 1992. Their son Benigno Aquino III was president from 2010 to 2016. The center's strength is that it follows all three eras in one place.

The museum stands in Barangay San Miguel, Tarlac City, along Luisita Industrial Park Road, inside the Cojuangco family's Hacienda Luisita. It is some distance from the San Sebastian Cathedral area in the city center, so plan the transfer separately. According to Wikipedia, work on the center began in 1993, inspired by the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum in Boston. The foundation raised about

from donors around the world, and the Cojuangco family donated a lot of about 5 hectares. The museum opened on August 21, 2001, the 18th anniversary of Ninoy's assassination, and Corazon Aquino attended the opening.

The building is a modern structure of concrete, steel and glass, U-shaped around a central lawn. It was designed by Dan Lichauco of the Francisco Mañosa firm, a nephew of Ninoy Aquino. The museum closed after the 2022 presidential election and reopened in February 2025 after roughly two years of renovation starting in 2023. News reports say February 24 and Wikipedia says February 25, a one-day difference, but either way it was just before the 39th anniversary of the EDSA Revolution. With the reopening, the 1987 Constitution exhibit was refurbished, the section on Corazon Aquino's post-presidency years was expanded, and a separate wing on the life and presidency of Benigno Aquino III was added. This guide is based on reopening reports, Wikipedia and a pre-renovation visitor account. Check the foundation's announcements before you go for current routes and guiding arrangements.

This section follows Ninoy's time as a Korean War correspondent, his entry into politics, his Senate career, his imprisonment and his 1983 assassination at Manila International Airport, in chronological order. A pre-renovation visitor account mentions a Rolleiflex camera and a replica of the Fort Bonifacio cell where he was held under Marcos. Check on site whether the same items are still displayed after the renovation.

Wikipedia says the jacket Ninoy wore when he was shot, stained with blood, along with his belt and boots, is on display. These items are regarded as the center's symbol and put a moment of modern history in front of you. The mood is heavy, so if you bring children, tell them in advance.

blocks.title: Corazon Aquino and the EDSA Revolution

children.text: This section covers how Corazon Aquino entered politics after her husband's death, became president through the 1986 EDSA People Power Revolution, served as president and was active afterward. Reports on the reopening say the section on her post-presidency years was expanded.

This area was refurbished during the renovation. You can see the background against which the 1987 Constitution was written under Corazon Aquino's government. It is a useful resource for travelers who want to understand the Philippine political system.

This wing, newly opened with the reopening, presents the life and presidency of Benigno Aquino III. For the opening, the photobook PNoy: Filipino, a visual retrospective of his presidency, was introduced.

According to a pre-renovation visitor account, a short film was shown in a small theater before the guided tour, and the shorter film Ninoy: the Heart and the Soul was screened often. It has not been confirmed whether the same arrangement continues after the renovation.

Even apart from the exhibits, the architecture is worth a look. The modern concrete, steel and glass building wraps around a lawn, and it has been described as the hall that displayed entries from an art contest themed on Ninoy's jacket.

items.title: Half-Day Course
items.subtitle: From the city to San Miguel and the museum

children.text: Leave from your hotel or bus terminal in Tarlac City. Give the full name,
Aquino Center and Museum (San Miguel, Luisita)
, to your driver and save it in your map app.

On arrival, check the admission fee and current visiting hours at the entrance. Right after the reopening, an announcement said it was open only in the afternoon, so it is safest to check notices for your visit date in advance.
Start with the Ninoy exhibit and go through in chronological order. If there is a film screening, watch it first.
See the Corazon Aquino exhibit and the 1987 Constitution exhibit.
See the Benigno Aquino III wing, then look around the lawn and the building's exterior.
Have lunch near Luisita or back in the city, and if time remains, continue to the cathedral area in Tarlac City.
These times are only an example, since opening hours may be afternoon-focused after the renovation. Adjust them to the actual opening hours.

items.title: Full History Day
items.subtitle: Combining the museum with cultural sites in the city

children.text: Have breakfast in Tarlac City and look around San Sebastian Cathedral.
Head toward San Miguel by tricycle or car. Check your destination on the map again along the way.
On arrival at the museum, check the opening hours and admission fee, then view the exhibits.
After your visit, rest while looking at the lawn and the building's exterior, then return to the city.
If time remains, look around other cultural sites or the market in the city, then go to the terminal in time for your bus to Manila.
Rather than trying to fit in two or more places in a day, it is better to build the day around the museum and use any spare time for the rest.
Several bus operators run from Manila to Tarlac City, and travel time varies greatly with traffic. Check the operator's latest announcements for terminal locations and timetables.
From the Tarlac City terminal, transfer to a tricycle or jeepney heading toward San Miguel, or use a ride-hailing app. Check the route and fare for this stretch locally.
Even if your ticket says Tarlac, it can differ whether the bus enters the city or lets you off on the expressway, so confirm the drop-off point with the conductor.
From Clark International Airport (CRK) to Tarlac City you travel overland, and regular transport options should be checked locally.
If you are in a group, consider a rental car or a hailed taxi all the way to San Miguel.
The city center around San Sebastian Cathedral and San Miguel are not within walking distance, so use a tricycle or a car.
When you board, state your destination and whether the driver should wait for the return trip, and agree on the fare first.
The Aquino Center is a different place from the military base Camp Servillano Aquino. Search for it on the map by its official name.
The museum is indoors, so you can visit year-round. However, Tarlac has distinct dry and rainy seasons, so the dry season is more convenient for getting around.

Events may be held around the EDSA Revolution anniversary (February 25) and the anniversary of Ninoy's assassination (August 21). The reopening was also timed to the EDSA commemoration. During event periods, visiting hours or arrangements may change, so check the latest announcements.
Allow about one to two hours for the exhibits, but more if you want to see the film screening and hear all the explanations. Including travel, half a day is about right.

You can find lodging in hotels in the Luisita area, where the Aquino Center is, or in Tarlac City. A 2014 visitor account mentioned a hotel close to the museum, but check whether it is still operating before booking. A day trip from Manila is possible, but allow generous travel time given the afternoon visiting hours.
Rather than eating inside the museum, it is better to eat near Luisita or in Tarlac City. Business conditions change often, so check the latest information in your map app.

For a day trip, you could eat an early lunch in Tarlac City and go to the museum in the afternoon. If opening hours have shifted to afternoons, the natural order is to see the cathedral area in the morning and go to San Miguel after lunch. If the 8 a.m. opening has been kept, seeing the museum first in the morning and then returning to the city is less hot. Either way, check the last bus back to Manila first and plan around it.

Opening hours differ by source. Travel information sites list daily 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., but reopening reports say 1 p.m. to 5:30 p.m. Check the latest announcement for your visit date through the foundation's Facebook page or by phone.

(seniors
, students
); no official notice was found and it may have changed after the 2025 reopening. Bring some small cash.
A pre-renovation visitor account mentioned rules on photography inside the exhibit halls. Follow the signs and staff instructions on site.
The exhibits cover Ninoy's assassination and the martial law period, so you need time to read the explanations. Explanations are mainly in English, so knowing the background beforehand helps.
Because it requires a separate trip from the cathedral area in the city, it is realistic to plan one day around the museum and one city site.
Before you arrive, check the name on the map to make sure your navigation is not sending you to Camp Aquino or another Aquino memorial site.
If children are with you, tell them in advance that the exhibits include bloodstained items.
Explanations may be mainly in English. Knowing Philippine modern history terms (martial law, EDSA, People Power) beforehand helps.
Reports say it was open only in the afternoon just after the reopening, so be sure to check opening hours before a morning visit.
Admission, opening hours and photography rules come from a 2014 visitor account and travel sites, so they may differ from current ones.
Sources differ on the reopening date, February 24 or 25, so this guide does not state an exact date.
San Miguel is away from the city center, so arrange your return transport in advance.
As a private foundation museum, it may close on holidays or for events. Contact them before visiting.
The exhibits deal with politically sensitive subjects. Avoid loud arguments while visiting.
A city course with San Sebastian Cathedral and cultural sites in the city center, requiring a separate trip from the museum.
A memorial tied to the Bataan Death March in World War II, which can extend a modern history trip.
A monastery pilgrimage site near San Jose, best planned as a separate half-day course.
The signature trek of the Tarlac and Zambales area; better not to combine it with the Aquino Center on the same day.
